newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF team sees tough problems to be solved in Sofia.
newsitem.headline: IMF team sees tough problems to be solved in Sofia.

text.p: International Monetary Fund (IMF) negotiators said on Monday they face hard problems before reaching a funding agreement that would help Bulgaria stabilise its crumbling economy.

"We have a lot of complex issues to solve before we can be confident of setting up a currency board and all the supporting measures. There are very difficult problems to solve in the budget," IMF mission leader Anne McGuirk said on arrival as Sofia Airport.
"We hope it will not take too long. We think there is a willingness to deal with all these issues and so we are here to work hard," she told reporters.
McGuirk arrived from Brussels where the European Union discussed mobilising help for the crisis-torn country, but the EU decided to act after an agreement with the IMF was in place.

"They are all prepared to suport Bulgaria once we have a programme and they have agreed to hold a G-24 (group of industrialy advanced nations) meeting to raise financial support as soon as we can agree on a programme," McGuirk said.

The team is expected to review Bulgaria's dramatically slumping economy and set arrangements for a currency board system, proposed last year to halt the freefall of the lev and to restore confidence in its ailing banks.

The system requires levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely curbing financial powers of the government and the central bank, thus preventing printing of money. It will entail closure of inefficient state enterprises and more job losses.
"We are very favourably impressed by the steps the government has already taken and the commitment to reforms," McGuirk said.
Delayed reform and mismanagement by the previous Socialist administration have thrown Bulgaria's economy into chaos, while 30 days of widespread strikes and political squabbling further paralysed it.
Three weeks ago President Petar Stoyanov mediated an agreement to hold a general election on April 19, dissolved parliament and named an interim cabinet headed by Sofia mayor Stefan Sofianski.
"We can work with an interim government," McGuirk, whose first meeting on Tuesday is with Sofianski, said.
One of the last items voted by the outgoing parliament was to expand powers of the interim cabinet to negotiate vital loans and agreements with multilateral lending institutions.
The system's introduction, however, would require amendments to banking laws be passed by the new parliament, which must also decide whether to peg the lev to the dollar or the mark.
The Fund and government will also need to seek means to resolve Bulgaria's 1.7 trillion lev domestic debt, seen as a hindrance to successful implementation of the currency board.

Passing a realistic austerity budget for this year will be one of the first tasks of the new parliament, once elected. Bulgaria's deepening crisis has made obsolete the 1997 budget assumptions drafted by the former Socialist government.

The currency has fallen by some 300 percent against the dollar since the beginning of the year and economists see February inflation at around 100 percent. Monthly inflation last month was 44 percent.
Central bank governor Lyubomir Filipov saw June as the earliest date for the system's introduction.

On Sunday the World Bank said it had $200 million available for Bulgaria if the government speeded up privatisation and closures of loss-making state firms, and lifted price controls on basic goods and services. ($=2,195 lev).
